title: Biodiversity, GMOs, Nano World, Gene Therapy & Climate Change
subject: Science, Technology, and Society
description: Linnaeus's taxonomy & 2010 Biodiversity Year, Biotechnology/GMOs/Cartagena Protocol/Golden Rice, Nanoscale (10⁻⁹ m), Gene Therapy & Stem Cell cautions (Dr. Samuel Bernal), and Climate Change (Milankovitch parameters, Chaos Theory, Tyndall, Keeling Curve & tipping points).
sourceFile: STS-WK1-MTWThF A book reference in STS.pdf, STS MIDTERM REVIEWER.docx

questions.question: Who devised the hierarchical system of taxonomy still used today to classify and name living organisms, reflecting 'the One in the Many'?
options: Charles Darwin
Carl Linnaeus (Swedish scientist)
Louis Pasteur
Milutin Milankovitch
questions.answer: Carl Linnaeus (Swedish scientist)
questions.explanation: Linnaeus's taxonomy groups diverse species under shared genera, showing how living things are interrelated.

questions.question: Roughly how many species have been identified so far on Earth, how many total are estimated, and what year did the UN declare the International Year of Biodiversity?
options: ~1.75 million identified (out of ~13 million estimated, ranging 3–100M); 2010
~100,000 identified; 1995
~50 million identified; 2020
~500 identified; 1948
questions.answer: ~1.75 million identified (out of ~13 million estimated, ranging 3–100M); 2010
questions.explanation: On December 20, 2006, the UN General Assembly declared 2010 the International Year of Biodiversity to raise awareness of species loss.

questions.question: How do 'biotechnology' and 'genetic engineering' differ according to the Biodiversity International module (Bragdon et al., 2005)?
options: Biotechnology uses biological systems/organisms/derivatives to make or modify products; genetic engineering transfers genes/DNA between sources to create LMOs/GMOs
Biotechnology only builds computers; genetic engineering only studies rocks
They are banned under the UN Charter
Genetic engineering existed in ancient Sumeria
questions.answer: Biotechnology uses biological systems/organisms/derivatives to make or modify products; genetic engineering transfers genes/DNA between sources to create LMOs/GMOs
questions.explanation: Recombinant DNA (gene splicing / transgenic technology) inserts selected trait genes from one species into an unrelated organism.

questions.question: During genetic modification (recombinant DNA technology), what is actually transferred from one organism into the host organism?
options: The entire brain of the donor animal
Only specific isolated sections of a gene carrying the desired trait (not the whole DNA)
Whole organs transplanted surgically
Artificial plastic polymers
questions.answer: Only specific isolated sections of a gene carrying the desired trait (not the whole DNA)
questions.explanation: A desired trait gene is identified, isolated, replicated, and inserted so the modified organism grows and replicates with that trait.

questions.question: According to Nicholson (2014) in Chapter 9, how can GMO corporate patents threaten 'farmer sovereignty' and food security?
options: Companies holding GMO patents can sue farmers whose fields become contaminated by drifting pollen/seeds from neighboring farms
Patents force all crops to grow twice as slowly
Patents prevent sunlight from reaching farms
Farmers are paid too much money by biotech firms
questions.answer: Companies holding GMO patents can sue farmers whose fields become contaminated by drifting pollen/seeds from neighboring farms
questions.explanation: Alongside ecological disruption and biodiversity loss, corporate seed monopolies and patent lawsuits raise major ethical concerns.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (signed by the Philippines)?
options: To ban all agriculture in biodiversity hotspots
To take a precautionary approach ensuring safe handling, transport, and informed consent before importing LMOs/GMOs that might harm biodiversity or human health
To set global fossil-fuel emission quotas
To regulate stem cell beauty clinics in Manila
questions.answer: To take a precautionary approach ensuring safe handling, transport, and informed consent before importing LMOs/GMOs that might harm biodiversity or human health
questions.explanation: Because the Philippines is a global biodiversity hotspot, the Cartagena Protocol provides vital biosafety data before LMO imports.

questions.question: What nutrient was Golden Rice genetically engineered to provide, and what did Glenn Stone's Washington University study (reported by Gerry Everding, 2016) conclude?
options: Vitamin C; it cured malaria by 2005
Vitamin A (beta-carotene); Golden Rice was still not market-ready and environmental activists were not mainly responsible for its slow rollout
Protein; farmers grew rich overnight
Calcium; it replaced all vegetables in Asia
questions.answer: Vitamin A (beta-carotene); Golden Rice was still not market-ready and environmental activists were not mainly responsible for its slow rollout
questions.explanation: Heralded in 2000 for Vitamin A deficiency, Golden Rice faced scientific/breeding hurdles and remained controversial over corporate GMO adoption.

questions.question: What mathematical scale does the prefix 'nano' represent, and roughly how wide is a single strand of DNA?
options: One millionth (10⁻⁶); 100 nanometers
One billionth (10⁻⁹) of a meter; about 3 nanometers wide
One thousandth (10⁻³); 1 millimeter
One trillionth (10⁻¹²); 50 micrometers
questions.answer: One billionth (10⁻⁹) of a meter; about 3 nanometers wide
questions.explanation: A nanometer is 10⁻⁹ meters—DNA is ~3 nm wide, an aspirin molecule is ~0.5 nm, and a small nanoparticle is ~5 nm.

questions.question: In Figure 3.10 (US EPA), how do human hair (50–70 µm), fine beach sand (90 µm), PM₁₀, and PM₂.₅ compare in size?
options: PM₂.₅ (<2.5 µm) and PM₁₀ (<10 µm) are far smaller than human hair (50–70 µm) and beach sand (90 µm)
PM₂.₅ is larger than a grain of beach sand
Human hair is smaller than a single atom
Pollen grains are ten times larger than beach sand
questions.answer: PM₂.₅ (<2.5 µm) and PM₁₀ (<10 µm) are far smaller than human hair (50–70 µm) and beach sand (90 µm)
questions.explanation: The text also notes a particle of beach sand is almost ten times larger than a pollen grain.

questions.question: What is nanotechnology, and which current innovations are cited in Chapter 10?
options: Manipulation of matter on an atomic or subatomic scale; innovations include microprocessors and strain-resistant fabrics
Giant hydroelectric dam engineering
Open-pit coal mining
Traditional handloom textile dyeing
questions.answer: Manipulation of matter on an atomic or subatomic scale; innovations include microprocessors and strain-resistant fabrics
questions.explanation: Specialized microscopes unlocked the nano world, promising breakthroughs in health, environment, and security.

questions.question: In Chapter 11, how is gene therapy conceptually explained for countering a condition like cancer cell growth?
options: Finding the harmful gene among the 46 chromosomal structures, removing the faulty section, and replacing it with a 'correct' gene part
Replacing all blood cells with plastic nanoparticles
Exposing the patient to ultraviolet X-rays daily
Removing all 46 chromosomes permanently
questions.answer: Finding the harmful gene among the 46 chromosomal structures, removing the faulty section, and replacing it with a 'correct' gene part
questions.explanation: Gene therapy corrects genetic misinformation at the molecular level, though high expertise makes it financially costly.

questions.question: In Totel de Jesus's article ('What we should know about stem cell treatment in the PH'), what cautions did Dr. Samuel Bernal emphasize?
options: Stem-cell therapy is NOT a 'cure-all' or anti-aging fountain of youth—it tries to help the body heal itself at the molecular level, and patients must beware fly-by-night clinics
Every beauty clinic in Manila is FDA-approved for anti-aging miracles
Stem cells replace the need for medical diagnosis
Stem cell therapy works instantly without scientific oversight
questions.answer: Stem-cell therapy is NOT a 'cure-all' or anti-aging fountain of youth—it tries to help the body heal itself at the molecular level, and patients must beware fly-by-night clinics
questions.explanation: Dr. Samuel Bernal (doctor-lawyer in regenerative medicine & FDA/FTC regulation) urged strict scientific and legal caution.

questions.question: In Chapter 11's genetic code table, how many total three-nucleotide codons exist, how many encode the 20 amino acids, and what are the four DNA nucleotides?
options: 64 total codons; 61 encode the 20 amino acids (plus 3 STOP codons); Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Thymine (T)
20 total codons; 10 encode proteins; A, B, C, D
46 total codons; 40 encode fats; U, V, W, X
100 total codons; 64 encode sugars; A, G, C, Z
questions.answer: 64 total codons; 61 encode the 20 amino acids (plus 3 STOP codons); Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Thymine (T)
questions.explanation: Because 61 codons map to 20 amino acids, most amino acids are encoded by more than one codon (e.g., ATG = Met*, TAA/TAG/TGA = STOP).

questions.question: How does Chapter 12 distinguish 'climate' from 'weather,' and what is the Greek origin of 'climate'?
options: Weather changes constantly day-to-day, while climate refers to long-term prevailing atmospheric patterns; from Greek klinein ('to slope') -> klima
Climate lasts one hour; weather lasts a century
Both mean exactly the same thing in meteorology
Climate comes from Latin scire ('to know')
questions.answer: Weather changes constantly day-to-day, while climate refers to long-term prevailing atmospheric patterns; from Greek klinein ('to slope') -> klima
questions.explanation: Ancient Greeks noticed noon sun angle sloped lower and air grew colder sailing northward, coining klima.

questions.question: In Earth's elliptical orbit around the Sun, what are 'aphelion' and 'perihelion'?
options: Aphelion: point farthest from the Sun; Perihelion: point closest to the Sun
Aphelion: point closest to the Sun; Perihelion: point farthest from the Sun
Aphelion: North Pole tilt; Perihelion: equator line
Aphelion: longest day; Perihelion: shortest day
questions.answer: Aphelion: point farthest from the Sun; Perihelion: point closest to the Sun
questions.explanation: Remember: 'P' for Perihelion = Proximity (closest); 'A' for Aphelion = Away (farthest).

questions.question: What distinguishes an 'equinox' from a 'solstice'?
options: Equinox: sun at noon is directly over the equator (2x/year, equal day & night); Solstice: sun sits above Tropic of Cancer or Capricorn (longest or shortest daylight)
Equinox occurs only in winter; solstice occurs every month
Equinox happens every 23,000 years; solstice happens once a century
Both occur when the Moon blocks the Sun
questions.answer: Equinox: sun at noon is directly over the equator (2x/year, equal day & night); Solstice: sun sits above Tropic of Cancer or Capricorn (longest or shortest daylight)
questions.explanation: Earth's axial tilt causes changing solar angles across equinoxes and solstices.

questions.question: What is 'precession,' and roughly how many years does one full cycle of the precession of the equinoxes take to return to its modern position?
options: Gradual wobbling change in Earth's rotational axis orientation (like a spinning trumpo); ~23,000 years
Sudden reversal of ocean currents; 10 years
Daily spin of Earth; 24 hours
Monthly lunar phase; 29 days
questions.answer: Gradual wobbling change in Earth's rotational axis orientation (like a spinning trumpo); ~23,000 years
questions.explanation: Figure 3.13 illustrates the 23,000-year precession cycle shifting which seasons align with perihelion and aphelion.

questions.question: Who investigated in the 1930s whether long-term solar-orbital variations could trigger Ice Ages, and what three factors are now called the Milankovitch parameters?
options: Slovak scientist Milutin Milankovitch; 1) change in Earth's orbital radius/eccentricity, 2) change in axial tilt, and 3) wobble (precession) in the spin axis
John Tyndall; coal, methane, and water vapor
Charles Keeling; latitude, altitude, and ocean depth
Carl Linnaeus; kingdom, phylum, and species
questions.answer: Slovak scientist Milutin Milankovitch; 1) change in Earth's orbital radius/eccentricity, 2) change in axial tilt, and 3) wobble (precession) in the spin axis
questions.explanation: Milankovitch calculated these orbital variations over thousands of years, though he lacked computers to verify their full non-linear impact.

questions.question: Why did contemporaries initially reject Milankovitch's theory, and what later mathematical science (linked to Henri Poincaré and computers) validated its cumulative impact?
options: Critics thought each effect was too tiny to matter; Chaos Theory showed non-linear cumulative changes over millennia can trigger massive climate shifts like Ice Ages
Critics proved Earth has no axial tilt; Algebra disproved it
Critics banned trigonometry; Quantum mechanics solved it
Milankovitch never wrote down any equations
questions.answer: Critics thought each effect was too tiny to matter; Chaos Theory showed non-linear cumulative changes over millennia can trigger massive climate shifts like Ice Ages
questions.explanation: Computers confirmed Poincaré's insight that summing non-linear effects can produce far greater outcomes than simple linear addition.

questions.question: According to Figure 3.16 in Chapter 12, when did atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentration shift from fairly constant to a sharp, steep climb alongside rising global temperature?
options: Around 1950 and sharply into the 21st century
During the 11th century (1000 CE)
During the 15th century
It dropped to zero after 1950
questions.answer: Around 1950 and sharply into the 21st century
questions.explanation: While debate exists between purely natural vs. human-driven causes, the post-1950 spike in CO₂ and temperature threatens irreversible instability.

questions.question: How did 19th-century British engineer John Tyndall (1859) describe the natural greenhouse effect, and why is it essential for life on Earth?
options: Like a dam deepening a river, atmospheric gases trap outgoing infrared heat—keeping Earth warm and livable instead of frozen like Mars or Antarctica
Like a giant refrigerator cooling the equator
It blocks all visible sunlight from reaching plants
It turns oceans into solid ice
questions.answer: Like a dam deepening a river, atmospheric gases trap outgoing infrared heat—keeping Earth warm and livable instead of frozen like Mars or Antarctica
questions.explanation: Tyndall noted water vapor was then the most prevalent greenhouse gas, while worrying about future fossil-fuel CO₂ from industrialization.

questions.question: Who began measuring atmospheric CO₂ continuously in 1958 atop Mauna Loa in Hawaii (far from factories), and what did the 'Keeling Curve' reveal?
options: Charles David Keeling; CO₂ concentrations steadily climbed (reaching 410.52 ppm by May 2017) alongside rising temperatures
John Tyndall; CO₂ disappeared after WWII
Milutin Milankovitch; Hawaii had zero CO₂
Isaac Newton; CO₂ only changes during solstices
questions.answer: Charles David Keeling; CO₂ concentrations steadily climbed (reaching 410.52 ppm by May 2017) alongside rising temperatures
questions.explanation: The Keeling Curve confirmed Tyndall's 1859 concern that post-WWII industrialization substantially raised global atmospheric CO₂.

questions.question: In chaos theory and climate modeling, what is a 'tipping point'?
options: The exact date winter turns to spring
A threshold value of meteorological parameters beyond which irreversible changes replace the old climate state with an uncertain chaotic regime
The top of a mountain thermometer
A tax incentive for coal power plants
questions.answer: A threshold value of meteorological parameters beyond which irreversible changes replace the old climate state with an uncertain chaotic regime
questions.explanation: Because climate is a chaotic system, accurate global data is vital for computer models predicting tipping points.

questions.question: What central policy dilemma does Chapter 12 highlight regarding fossil fuels, industrialization, and climate change?
options: Fossil fuels are currently a major electricity source for modernization/industrialization, yet burning them increases CO₂—requiring a balanced plan protecting both economy and environment
Countries must stop using all electricity immediately
CO₂ has zero connection to fossil fuels
Science is a rigid blueprint that never adapts
questions.answer: Fossil fuels are currently a major electricity source for modernization/industrialization, yet burning them increases CO₂—requiring a balanced plan protecting both economy and environment
questions.explanation: Chapter 12 concludes that 'science is more like a cookbook than a blueprint'—open to experimentation, refinement, and wise judgment.

questions.question: In a biodiverse ecosystem where organisms must survive on limited resources (Chapter 9), how do multiple species coexist?
options: They ignore each other completely
Available energy is shared and passed among species through diverse ecological relationships
Only one species is permitted per continent
Plants produce electricity for animals
questions.answer: Available energy is shared and passed among species through diverse ecological relationships
questions.explanation: Biodiversity underpins essential ecological functions, food supplies, medicines, timber, and resilience.

questions.question: Which of the following is a stated goal of modern biotechnology in food and agriculture (Bragdon et al., 2005)?
options: Developing pest- and disease-resistant crops, combating drought/salinity, enhancing nutritional quality, and reducing production inputs
Eliminating all crop varieties down to one plant
Increasing soil toxicity deliberately
Replacing photosynthesis with diesel
questions.answer: Developing pest- and disease-resistant crops, combating drought/salinity, enhancing nutritional quality, and reducing production inputs
questions.explanation: Modern biotechnology offers powerful molecular tools for agriculture, balanced against biosafety and equity concerns.

questions.question: Why is biodiversity loss considered a direct threat to human society and health?
options: It threatens food supplies, sources of medicines, wood, energy, recreation, and essential ecological functions
It only affects museum ticket prices
It increases planetary biocapacity automatically
It stops Earth's axial precession
questions.answer: It threatens food supplies, sources of medicines, wood, energy, recreation, and essential ecological functions
questions.explanation: Society, the environment, and human health are deeply interconnected.

questions.question: Why was the nano world unrecognized by early civilizations until specialized microscopes were developed?
options: Because nanostructures (measured in 10⁻⁹ meters) are far too tiny to be seen by the naked eye
Because nanoparticles only exist on Mars
Because atoms were invented in 1995
Because light cannot reflect off carbon
questions.answer: Because nanostructures (measured in 10⁻⁹ meters) are far too tiny to be seen by the naked eye
questions.explanation: Even natural catalysts, minerals, and DNA (~3 nm wide) operate invisibly at the nanoscale.

questions.question: In Chapter 12, what scientific caution is raised when interpreting the strong correlation between rising atmospheric CO₂ and rising global temperature?
options: Correlation alone does not automatically prove cause-and-effect—scientists had to turn to historical data and physics to substantiate the causal link
Correlation means CO₂ lowers global temperature
Scientists ignore all historical climate records
Temperature cannot be measured accurately
questions.answer: Correlation alone does not automatically prove cause-and-effect—scientists had to turn to historical data and physics to substantiate the causal link
questions.explanation: Distinguishing correlation from causation is fundamental to rigorous climate science.

questions.question: Why are genetically modified organisms (GMOs) also referred to as 'transgenic' organisms?
options: Because they travel across continents by ship
Because genetic engineering transfers ('trans-') genes from the DNA of one species into an unrelated organism
Because they have zero DNA inside their cells
Because they are grown without soil
questions.answer: Because genetic engineering transfers ('trans-') genes from the DNA of one species into an unrelated organism
questions.explanation: Transgenic crops borrow specific trait-bearing gene sections from another species via recombinant DNA.

questions.question: What example does Chapter 11 use to show how 'old' medical breakthroughs connect to modern nano and gene science?
options: Aspirin—known for relieving pain long before its ~0.5 nm molecular structure was understood at the nanoscale
The bamboo laundry-basket incubator
The Gutenberg metal printing press
The Salamander amphibious tricycle
questions.answer: Aspirin—known for relieving pain long before its ~0.5 nm molecular structure was understood at the nanoscale
questions.explanation: Applying molecular and atomic insights to genes opens new frontiers in targeted human healthcare.

questions.question: How did post-WWII industrialization dramatically change atmospheric CO₂ compared to John Tyndall's mid-19th-century observations?
options: Widespread agrarian economies converted into large-scale coal- and fossil-fuel-powered industries, releasing huge amounts of CO₂ as a by-product
Industrialization eliminated all fossil fuel burning
Agrarian farms emitted more coal smoke than modern factories
Post-WWII factories ran exclusively on saltwater lamps
questions.answer: Widespread agrarian economies converted into large-scale coal- and fossil-fuel-powered industries, releasing huge amounts of CO₂ as a by-product
questions.explanation: Rapid global industrialization turned Tyndall's theoretical warning into measurable atmospheric change.

questions.question: What important reminder does Chapter 12 give regarding carbon dioxide (CO₂) and other greenhouse gases?
options: While CO₂ is a primary indicator of global warming, it is NOT the only greenhouse gas (water vapor, for example, is prevalent too)
CO₂ is the only gas present in Earth's atmosphere
Oxygen causes 100% of the greenhouse effect
Greenhouse gases freeze the oceans
questions.answer: While CO₂ is a primary indicator of global warming, it is NOT the only greenhouse gas (water vapor, for example, is prevalent too)
questions.explanation: Multiple greenhouse gases trap infrared radiation, though rising fossil-fuel CO₂ drives modern warming concern.

questions.question: In Chapter 10's activity on George Tulevski's TED Talk, why is nature cited as an inspiration for nanotechnology?
options: Nature builds complex living organisms from the bottom up, molecule by molecule and atom by atom
Nature only uses large concrete blocks
Nature avoids chemical bonding
Nature operates exclusively at kilometer scales
questions.answer: Nature builds complex living organisms from the bottom up, molecule by molecule and atom by atom
questions.explanation: Chemistry and self-assembly teach nanotechnologists how to construct functional structures from atomic building blocks.

questions.question: Why does the conclusion of Chapter 12 compare science to 'a cookbook rather than a blueprint'?
options: Because science is open to experimentation, innovation, and refinement—requiring wise judgment ('a fine sense of taste') rather than rigid blind formulas
Because scientists only study culinary arts
Because blueprints cannot be drawn by hand
Because experiments never need data
questions.answer: Because science is open to experimentation, innovation, and refinement—requiring wise judgment ('a fine sense of taste') rather than rigid blind formulas
questions.explanation: Living the good life in an age of rapid S&T demands both scientific rigor and ethical wisdom.
